item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Fat Joe’sEx-Hypeman Seeks Free Lawyer To Fight Defamation Case
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Fat Joe's former collaborator asks the court for volunteer counsel as he prepares a bid to end the defamation suit.
item.content:encoded:
Fat Joe‘s former hypeman wants a volunteer lawyer to help him seek judgment without a trial in the rapper’s defamation lawsuit.

Terrance Dixon submitted the request ahead of a November 13 deadline to address his representation after Tyrone Blackburn left his legal team.

The request follows Judge Jennifer E. Willis’ October 2 decision allowing Blackburn to withdraw from Dixon’s two linked cases. Her order offered Dixon three choices: hire another lawyer, represent himself or request volunteer counsel.

In a November 12 application filed in Manhattan federal court, Dixon outlined his next move against his former boss. He also submitted a separate application asking to proceed without prepaying court fees or costs.

“I need an attorney because discovery has ended and I want to move for summary judgment,” Dixon wrote. “I have not yet asked for an attorney in this case because I was previously represented by Tyrone Blackburn, who is also a defendant in this case. However, he withdrew and the court gave until Nov. 13 for me to find another attorney or submit an application for pro bono counsel.”

Dixon said he had sought assistance from the City Bar Justice Center’s Pro Se Clinic. He described a limit on the help it could provide for the motion he wants to file.

“I have contacted the Pro Se Clinic at the City Bar Justice Center and have had calls about my case and next steps with them,” Dixon wrote. “They stated that they did not have the resources to assist me in drafting my motion for summary judgment and usually only help plaintiffs oppose summary judgment. They have assisted me in filling out this application.”

Fat Joe sued Dixon and Blackburn in April 2025, alleging they tried to extract money through false accusations. Dixon later brought his own lawsuit alleging abuse and unpaid work, claims the rapper denied.

Blackburn’s withdrawal did not remove him as a defendant or end the court’s authority over pending sanctions matters. The October order paused issues involving Dixon through November 13.

Even if the court approves Dixon’s request, an attorney must volunteer to take the case.

item.title: Archie Eversole’s Brother Sees Murder Charges Dropped Days Before Trial
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Archie Eversole's brother avoids a murder trial as prosecutors say their latest review cannot support a conviction.
item.content:encoded:
Archie Eversole‘s brother will no longer face a murder trial over the Atlanta rapper’s death, ending a prosecution that stretched more than four years and was headed toward a courtroom next week.

Alexander Krause, 46, had been awaiting trial on charges stemming from the 2022 shooting. The DeKalb County District Attorney’s Office announced Friday that it was dropping every count because prosecutors could not establish his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, according to WSB-TV’s reporting.

“Our decision in this matter reflects our commitment to justice, fairness, and transparency,” the DA’s office said.

A review undertaken as prosecutors prepared for trial changed their assessment of the evidence. The office said investigators found no evidence of a dispute between the brothers, while messages recovered from Eversole’s phone supported accounts that they had a good relationship.

The DA’s office also described limits to what forensic testing established. Prosecutors said a weapon the brothers jointly owned contained DNA from both men, and the evidence did not eliminate the reasonable possibility of a self-inflicted injury.

The dismissal follows an April 2023 indictment charging Krause with malice murder, felony murder, aggravated assault and a firearm offense. He had been released on bond in August 2022 while the case remained pending.

Questions about identification were part of the proceedings long before Friday’s announcement. Prosecutors previously said Eversole made statements pointing to his brother, but defense attorney David Schnipper disputed that account and argued that Eversole never identified Krause as the shooter.

Eversole was wounded on March 25, 2022, at the home he shared with his brother and sought help at a nearby gas station. He later died in the hospital at 37.

His music had already become part of Atlanta’s sports culture. “We Ready,” recorded with Bubba Sparxxx, became a stadium staple, and Atlanta United embraced the track as part of its match-day atmosphere.

The club publicly mourned Eversole after his death, remembering an artist who supported the team before its inaugural season. His connection to its supporters extended well beyond the song’s original release.

Prosecutors prepared a nolle prosequi order to dismiss all charges.

item.title: Queen Latifah Questions Rock Hall’s Past As Her Induction Nears
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Queen Latifah celebrates her upcoming induction while remembering when a place in the Rock Hall felt out of reach.
item.content:encoded:
Queen Latifah is heading into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame with gratitude for her peers and questions about who the institution once overlooked. A new interview finds her celebrating an honor she never considered a realistic goal when she started rapping.

Speaking with Billboard ahead of Saturday’s ceremony, Latifah recalled how distant that recognition felt. She welcomed the Hall’s evolution while explaining why its earlier approach left her unconvinced.

“It’s interesting because, when we were growing up, being inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame wasn’t even something we really thought about. It felt like they were missing the mark. We made rock and roll, but we couldn’t get in. So, if there are no Black people in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, what kind of Rock & Roll Hall of Fame are you? It’s been amazing to watch them grow and change,” Latifah said.

Her criticism came with excitement about sharing the occasion with artists she admires. This year’s class includes Sade, Wu-Tang Clan and MC Lyte, putting several generations of Black music inside the same celebration.

Latifah also described an unusual feeling for someone accustomed to fighting for opportunities: this achievement arrived without a campaign. She recalled calling longtime business partner Shakim Compere after learning the news, with both enjoying recognition that hadn’t required their usual hustle.

The rapper made clear that her own success began with women who showed her what was possible. Watching MC Lyte rhyme at a young age helped Latifah imagine a place for herself in Hip-Hop.

“She was the blueprint for me. Salt-N-Pepa were the blueprint for me. They took us little baby acts on tour and taught us how to do things. I really appreciate them,” Latifah said.

That appreciation for earlier generations also runs through her housing work in Newark. Her mother Rita’s experience supporting children on a teacher’s income helped shape what Latifah wanted those apartments to offer.

Before sitcoms and movies expanded her reach, 1989’s “All Hail the Queen” introduced a rapper insisting women belonged at the center of the conversation. “Ladies First” and the later “U.N.I.T.Y.” gave that position a lasting musical foundation.

BET will premiere her housing documentary, “You Can Go Home Again,” on November 27.

item.title: Method Man & Redman Bring Their Friendship To UGG's First ALD Campaign
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Method Man and Redman link up for UGG and Aimé Leon Dore's debut slipper, with a Harlem shoot ahead of Thursday's release.
item.content:encoded:
Method Man and Redman are putting decades of shared history on camera for a new footwear campaign. UGG and Aimé Leon Dore have brought the pair together for the brands’ first collaboration, with a Harlem stoop replacing the stage.

The campaign introduces the UGG ALD Slipper through photographs and an unscripted conversation, according to Deckers Japan’s November 10 announcement. The company says the two discuss family, memories and their lives beyond music while wearing the new shoes.

That pairing has a history that stretches well beyond a fashion shoot. Their first joint album, Blackout!, arrived in 1999, and they carried their partnership into the 2001 comedy How High. By 2004, they were starring together in the Fox sitcom Method & Red.

Method Man previously explained why working with Redman translates across those different settings in a November 2021 AllHipHop interview. Discussing their reunion on Power Book II: Ghost, he credited his longtime collaborator with helping him become a better live performer.

“Redman is a consummate professional like myself. If anything, I owe him a lot because he actually showed me how to perform correctly on stage — whether people remember or not,” Method Man said in that interview.

“He had been in the game two years prior than what I had been. So, when you put us on screen, that resonates. We have chemistry,” Method Man added.

Their television reunion put that familiar partnership into a different kind of relationship. Method Man played attorney Davis Maclean, while Redman appeared as his incarcerated older brother, Theo Rollins, during the series’ second season.

For the new campaign, the footwear is a moccasin-inspired slipper made from full-grain leather with UGG branding alongside Aimé Leon Dore’s Queens Crest. The two color options are Coffee Bean and Goldenrod, and the collection is offered in both men’s and women’s styles.

Aimé Leon Dore also receives the photography and film credit for the campaign, bringing its own production to the collaboration. Teddy Santis founded the fashion label in New York City.

The slippers go on sale November 12 through Aimé Leon Dore’s website and flagship stores, selected UGG stores and retail partners worldwide.

item.title: Babyface Explains Why Publishing Money Pushes Singers Into Songwriting
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Babyface breaks down the royalty imbalance behind singers taking up songwriting and refuses to shut out new talent.
item.content:encoded:
Babyface says the push for singers to write their own records isn’t only about artistic independence.

Sometimes, the person behind the microphone wants the money going to somebody else’s pen.

During the November 10 episode of Baby, This Is Keke Palmer, he explained how publishing income could leave a songwriter better off than an artist who never became a major touring draw.

“Being the writer and being the publisher was no question, you know, where you would make most of the money,” Babyface said.

That frustration encouraged some performers to take over the writing, he explained. The results varied because a strong singing voice didn’t automatically mean strong songwriting.

Palmer raised the concern that artists increasingly feel they must do every job. Babyface resisted turning that concern into a rule about who should stay out of songwriting.

He remembered being discouraged about his own singing. Rather than closing doors on other artists, he acknowledged that a record he doubted could still become a hit.

The distinction matters because a finished track can involve two separate copyrights. One protects the composition, including its lyrics; the other protects a particular recording. Owning one does not automatically mean you own the other.

Those rights can belong to different people and be licensed separately.

A vocalist’s performance and a songwriter’s work may reach listeners together, but the law does not treat them as one interchangeable contribution.

Publishing also reaches beyond the first recorded version of a song. A new performer can record the same composition while creating a different sound recording. That separation helps explain why singing a hit and owning its writing are different business positions.

Babyface has worked on both sides of that divide for decades.

His solo catalog includes Tender Lover, The Day and For The Cool In You, alongside collaborations that keep him connected to younger performers.

He recently appeared alongside Jack Harlow in a new-music preview after Harlow shifted toward R&B.

His Girls Night Out collaborations also include Kehlani, Queen Naija and Ella Mai.

Babyface shared the 2024 Grammy for Best R&B Song as one of the writers of SZA’s “Snooze”.

item.title: Ice Cube Links Oprah Snub To Mike Epps’ Unscripted Movie Joke
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Ice Cube revisits his Oprah snub with Mike Epps and points to an unscripted movie line as a possible reason for it.
item.content:encoded:
Ice Cube isn’t claiming a feud with Oprah Winfrey, but he’s pointing to a joke from a Mike Epps movie as a possible issue.

The rapper revisited his absence from a “Barbershop” cast appearance while sitting beside the comedian who delivered the line.

During their November 11 “Club Shay Shay” interview with Shannon Sharpe, Cube said, “I ain’t got no beef with Oprah. None.” He then brought up “All About the Benjamins,” recalling an Oprah reference Epps made during the film’s fish-tank scene.

Epps’ character refuses to retrieve a gun from the tank, using a crude sexual comparison involving Winfrey to explain his reluctance.

Cube suggested the joke might explain why he wasn’t included when his “Barbershop” co-stars appeared on her talk show. The action comedy arrived in 2002, with Cube and Epps playing a bounty hunter and a hustler.

“That was not in the script, homie,” Cube said when the conversation turned to who supplied the joke. Epps addressed Winfrey directly: “Oprah, you know I love you.” He also recalled his mother’s fondness for her show.

Cube’s complaints about missing an Oprah appearance go back much further than this week’s interview.

His criticism was already public in 2006, when Ludacris was also challenging how the daytime host handled rappers visiting her program to discuss their film work.

Ludacris appeared with his “Crash” co-stars in October 2005 and later criticized how the interview was edited. Winfrey publicly rejected the idea that she disliked the music, naming artists she listened to as rappers questioned how they were treated on her show.

Cube had already moved from N.W.A into acting with John Singleton’s “Boyz n the Hood” in 1991. His later work with Epps stretched across “Next Friday,” “All About the Benjamins” and “Friday After Next,” combining written dialogue with room for the comedian’s improvisation.

Their newest interview also comes as they work toward another installment of the “Friday” franchise. Cube has said the story will determine who returns for “Last Friday,” while Epps has been hearing from people hoping to join the movie.

Cube and Epps have also launched “Listen and Laugh,” with Dr. Dre appearing as their podcast’s first guest.

item.title: Dolly Babe Almost Traded Rap For Nails Before Pink Blush Takes Off
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Dolly Babe says she considered a $700 nail class before recording Pink Blush on her phone and landing her breakout hit.
item.content:encoded:
Dolly Babe nearly traded rap for a nail technician course before a bedroom recording changed her plans. The Dallas rapper discussed her backup career in a V-103 interview with DJ Sturgess published Tuesday on its YouTube channel.

"So I was going to be a nail tech," Dolly said. She had searched Google for legitimate ways to make money and considered paying $700 for a class. The idea came while she was weighing a practical way to earn outside music.

Instead, she recorded "Pink Blush" on her phone while alone in her room. After years of studio sessions, she said she lacked the motivation to book another and released the recording without mixing or mastering.

"That was the fastest a song has ever moved for me," she told Sturgess. Earlier viral moments had failed to last, leaving her ready to stop making music.

The June 30 single became her summer breakout and later received a remix featuring Megan Thee Stallion. A November 9 HITS profile put its Hot 100 debut at No. 58 and reported 3.3 million monthly Spotify listeners. It also counted more than 17 million video views and celebrity engagement from Rihanna, Madonna and Janet Jackson.

Radio followed the online response, with the single impacting Urban stations September 21. HITS reported that it became the most added record at both Urban and Rhythmic radio, counting 42 Urban adds and 51 Rhythmic adds. Her music also appeared on Spotify playlists including New Music Friday, Feelin' Myself, New Joints and Most Necessary, the profile noted.

Her follow-up single "Hittin" arrived October 27 through Princess Pink LLC under an exclusive license to 300 Entertainment, with the streaming listing giving its running time as two minutes. The label has its own history with her remix collaborator: Megan was on its roster when Warner Music Group acquired 300 in December 2021.

Dolly also told Sturgess she was working on her first official project without committing to an imminent release. She wanted that debut to meet her standards before giving listeners a finished collection.

She named Beyoncé as the artist she most wanted to collaborate with.

item.title: Milagro Gramz Challenges Judge’s One-Sentence Ruling In Megan Thee Stallion Appeal
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Milagro Gramz presses her appeal over an unexplained ruling as Megan Thee Stallion's lawyers defend the $75,000 judgment.
item.content:encoded:
Milagro Gramz is putting a judge’s one-sentence rejection at the center of her latest fight with Megan Thee Stallion, arguing that an unexplained ruling leaves an important question about impartiality unanswered.

Her reply brief in the Eleventh Circuit challenges the denial of her request to reopen the judgment. The blogger says the appeals court cannot properly review that decision without knowing how the judge evaluated her conflict allegations.

“Public confidence is not restored by a paperless ‘denied,'” Milagro wrote.

The dispute concerns U.S. District Judge Cecilia Altonaga’s husband, George Mencio Jr., and his position at Holland & Knight. Milagro points to the firm’s representation of Roc Nation CEO Desiree Perez in separate litigation, alongside Megan’s trial testimony about conversations with Perez.

Those connections, Milagro argues, create an appearance problem even without proof of actual bias.

Megan’s lawyers already rejected that reasoning. They also argue that federal procedural rules permit judges to reject this type of motion without issuing a written opinion.

They say neither the judge’s husband nor his firm appeared in this lawsuit, and the connections Milagro describes do not justify undoing the result.

“The judge’s spouse did not appear in this case. His firm did not appear in this case,” Megan’s attorneys wrote.

The two sides also disagree about whether Milagro waited too long. She says supporters alerted her to the spouse-firm relationship on May 29, and she investigated before filing her motion on July 7.

Megan’s team argues that the information was public before trial and that Milagro raised the issue only after losing other attempts at relief. Milagro counters that public availability does not establish when she actually learned the relevant facts.

“A bond motion is not a recusal motion,” Milagro wrote, rejecting the suggestion that her earlier request concerning payment should have included this challenge.

AllHipHop previously covered her appeal following the bond dispute, part of the continuing battle over Megan’s $75,000 judgment.

Her challenge to the underlying judgment and this separate appeal have been consolidated for disposition.

item.title: Beastie Boys Take “Licensed To Ill” At 40 To Jon Stewart & SmartLess
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Beastie Boys line up two anniversary interviews as a new vinyl edition revisits the debut that took rap to No. 1.
item.content:encoded:
Beastie Boys are taking the 40th anniversary of Licensed to Ill to The Daily Show with Jon Stewart and the SmartLess podcast, with Ad-Rock and Mike D set for both appearances on November 16.

The conversations accompany a new edition of the album that first took rap to No. 1 on the Billboard 200.

The duo’s appearances are part of the anniversary campaign. Def Jam Recordings and UMe are preparing a two-LP Vinylphyle reissue for March 18, 2027, months after the original album’s November 15 birthday.

The new pressing also deals with a less visible part of keeping a 40-year-old record in circulation: aging master tapes. Sterling Sound engineer Joe Nino-Hernes worked from a high-resolution digital transfer of the original 1986 quarter-inch master rather than repeatedly running the tapes.

“It also allowed me to minimize handling of the tapes that have become fragile with time,” Nino-Hernes explained.

He said his chosen process preserved fidelity better than cutting from a second-generation analog copy. The transfer used the same machine and electronics he employs when cutting records.

Chuck D contributes fresh liner notes to the package, continuing a connection that reaches back well beyond this anniversary. The Public Enemy co-founder also honored the group when Beastie Boys entered the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2012.

Ad-Rock and Mike D attended that Cleveland ceremony without MCA, who was ill. The tribute performance featured The Roots, Travie McCoy and Kid Rock covering music from the group’s catalog.

Before those honors, the trio had opened for Madonna in 1985 and built its early recording career at Def Jam. Rick Rubin and the group produced Licensed to Ill, whose singles included “Brass Monkey,” “Paul Revere” and “No Sleep Till Brooklyn.”

The album received its RIAA Diamond certification in 2015. Later Beastie Boys albums Ill Communication and Hello Nasty also reached No. 1, extending their chart history beyond the debut.

The anniversary edition preserves its 13-song sequence across three sides, leaving the fourth for a band-logo etching rather than additional audio.

The package includes a four-panel insert reproducing scans of the original tape boxes.

item.title: Snow Tha Product Refuses To Stay Quiet For The Music Business
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Snow Tha Product weighs the career cost of speaking up as she balances community advocacy with running her own operation.
item.content:encoded:
Snow Tha Product isn’t letting the music business decide which communities she’s allowed to defend. She’s speaking up for women, Latino communities and queer people even when that choice can complicate her career.

In a November 9 interview with Remezcla, she connected that stance to everyday needs rather than industry approval. “I wish, you know, having clean water didn’t become political,” Snow Tha Product said.

The conversation also covered the doubts imposed on her as a first-generation Latina and what younger women might hear in her music. Snow wants them to trust themselves instead of absorbing other people’s limits.

Her new project, Next Time, Believe Me, opens with “Should’ve Been Worse,” a title that feeds directly into her thoughts about staying quiet. “They benefit from our silence. Just remember that,” Snow Tha Product told Remezcla.

She’s discussing those choices while running a business with family members on her team. Independence hasn’t removed the larger companies from the picture, and she said she still has to operate around their power.

That business question has followed her through more than one career chapter. Snow’s Atlantic Records signing in 2012 put her inside a major label after she built attention through her own releases.

“I just wanna be able to one day live happily ever after in my home and not feel like people are gonna come to attack us,” Snow tha Product said.

Back then, she was already making a point of protecting the brands she’d created before the deal. She kept its terms private while discussing a balance between her established identity and the opportunities a larger company could offer.

The latest release carries Snow Tha Product, Inc. on its recording copyright line, with Universal Music Latino handling distribution. Across 17 songs and roughly 40 minutes, the project brings several collaborators into that setup. Solo songs include “QUE TE DUELA,” “BESTIE” and “Come For Me,” with the sequence moving between English and Spanish titles across its November 6 full digital release.

Zhavia joins “Blame It On Me,” while Toni Romiti appears on “Was It Something?” Gera MX, Chuzzington and AJ Hernz also appear, giving the middle of the tracklist a run of collaborations between Snow’s solo records.

Tech N9ne appears on the closing title track, which runs two minutes and three seconds.
